Subject: SLO measurement, alerting, and metrics access — short questionnaire

Hi Camila,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Procurement asked we send a short set of questions to validate how Redwood measures uptime/latency and what visibility we (NovaLabs) will get if we proceed. High level items below — a one-paragraph answer for each is perfect.

1) How do you measure availability and latency? What are the exact SLI definitions (p95/p99, windowing)?
2) What monitoring/alerting integration do you provide (pager, Slack, email)? Can we set our own alerts?
3) Will we get dashboard access to live and historic metrics? If so, what retention windows and what subsets of telemetry are available (per-route, per-model, per-token)?
4) What sampling is applied to metrics (especially for low-volume customers)?
5) For procurement: if we need a temporary exception (shorter retention or restricted dashboard access), what is the approval flow and expected lead time?

Can you also attach anything legal/procurement-friendly (one-sheet or packet) we can pass to our InfoSec and procurement teams?

Appreciate the quick turn — we are targeting an internal decision by next week.

Best,
Alice
Alice Chen
Sourcing Manager, NovaLabs

From: camila.reyes@redwood.com

Subject: Re: SLO measurement, alerting, and metrics access — short questionnaire

Hi Alice — thanks, and great to meet you yesterday. Short answers below and I attached a concise packet that procurement/InfoSec can use. Happy to hop on a 20-min call if anything needs more detail.

1) Measurement: Availability ("success rate") = percentage of requests that return a 200-range response within the configured timeout. Latency SLIs: p95 and p99 measured on request tail latency, computed over a rolling 5-minute window for alerting and a rolling 1-hour window for reporting. For contractual SLOs we calculate monthly aggregates using calendar-month windows (p95/p99 on server-side request latency excluding client timeouts).

2) Monitoring/alerting: We integrate with PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Slack, and email. Customers can create custom alerts in our dashboard and request webhook integrations. For escalations tied to SLAs we set up a runbook and escalation policy with on-call contacts during onboarding.

3) Dashboard access: We provide read-only Grafana dashboards with per-route and per-model views, and a CSV export for audit. Retention: 90 days of full-resolution metrics, 365 days of aggregated metrics (1-minute → 1-hour rollups). Per-token telemetry is available as aggregate counters; we do not export raw token payloads.

4) Sampling: For low-volume customers we use deterministic sampling for traces and adaptive sampling for detailed telemetry to preserve statistical accuracy on p95/p99 while keeping cost predictable. By default 100% of API request status and latency are recorded; traces are sampled at 10% with higher sampling on error spikes.

5) Temporary exceptions: Small exceptions (shorter retention, limited dashboard scope) can be approved by procurement + the security reviewer; typical lead time is 3–7 business days. Exceptions that affect contractual SLO measurement (e.g., disabling synthetic probes) require an engineering review and ~2 weeks for rollout, and are handled as a signed amendment.

Packet attached: "Redwood_SLO_Measurement_Packet_v2.pdf" (procurement-friendly summary + diagrams).

Next step: If this looks ok, we'll loop in our security lead to give your InfoSec a short walkthrough.

Best,
Camila Reyes
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: SLO measurement, alerting, and metrics access — short questionnaire

Adding a little technical nuance for InfoSec / platform teams to prevent misinterpretation when they read the packet:

- Measurement windows: For alerting we use rolling windows (5m) to detect rapid regressions and 1h for stabilization. Contracted SLOs are computed monthly; if a customer requests calendar-month exclusions (planned maintenance), we add standard exclusion windows documented in the addendum.
- Synthetic probing: We run internal synthetic probes from multiple regions at 1-min cadence for availability. These are used for health detection and are not included in customer request SLIs unless explicitly requested as part of a custom SLO.
- Aggregation semantics: p95/p99 are computed on server-side end-to-end latency (model decode included). We discard requests that hit client-side or gateway-level validation errors from SLI calculation.
- Dashboard entitlements: Customers receive RBAC'd read-only invites. We can create a scoped view for procurement that shows only monthly SLO summaries + incident timeline (if requested).

If procurement wants a temporary reduction of retention or to limit dashboard scope while they finalize data handling agreements, that is usually handled via a short internal ticket (I can triage) + procurement signoff. Engineers typically need 3–10 days depending on how scoped the change is.

-Mark

Hi Alice — quick answers inline below and I attached Grafana invite instructions for your ops folks.

A) Per-request token content: Confirmed — Redwood does not export or provide customer access to per-request token payloads or reconstructed prompt/completion texts. Customers receive aggregate counters (requests, tokens) and derived metrics (latency histograms, p95/p99) only. Any export of raw request content requires an approved legal/Privacy/Data Processing Addendum and is evaluated case-by-case.

B) Temporary retention exception: Confirmed path is: (1) procurement submits request and scope; (2) security reviews privacy impact; (3) engineering assesses implementation and cost; (4) procurement + engineering agree on duration and any fee; (5) signed addendum if required. Typical lead time for a scoped 45-day retention carveout is 5–10 business days. We generally charge a one-time configuration fee for custom retention behaviors; if the exception only involves dashboard visibility (no extra storage) we can often waive fees. We'll surface exact costs in the addendum.

Attached: "grafana-invite-instructions.txt" with steps to onboard your SREs and a read-only invite template.

Next step: If you want, I can open a HubSpot task and a short Jira ticket (ENG-4321) to track the exception request — that speeds the engineering review.

Thanks — Camila
